text: Bivariate analysis compares two variables at a time. It's where EDA starts producing the stories people care about: which customers spend more, which region churns most. The right technique depends on what types of variables you're pairing, so start by naming them.

Two numeric columns call for a scatter plot. Tenure against orders rises from lower left to upper right: longer tenure tends to mean more orders. The correlation is zero point five five, a moderate positive relationship.

To compare a number across categories, group and summarize. By channel, mean total spend looks like app customers are the big spenders, two thirty-two seventy. But the medians are nearly identical across all three channels, roughly one seventeen to one twenty-nine. Two huge spend values inflated the means of the groups they landed in.
That's the danger of comparing means when outliers are present: the difference you found may be two rows. Compare medians, or draw a box plot per group, before you believe a gap.

To relate two categorical columns, cross-tabulate and normalize by row to turn counts into rates. Churn rate by region: East fifteen point three percent, North nineteen point three, West twenty-one point five, South twenty-nine point three. South looks noticeably higher than East.

Before reporting that South churns more, ask two questions. How many customers are in each group? South has only ninety-nine, fewer than the others, so its rate can swing more. And could the difference be random? Treat it as a lead worth testing, not a conclusion, and remember: association is not causation.

Match the technique to the variable types: scatter for two numerics, grouped summaries for numeric versus category, crosstab for two categoricals. Always check group sizes before trusting a difference. Next: multivariate exploration, where three or more variables come into play.
